# Benchmark results {#results}

*Which method survives?*

Everything up to here was construction. Part I built a manifold whose exact
two-dimensional embedding is known in closed form, Part II put the method
families in front of it one at a time, Chapter \@ref(benchmarks) turned the
construction into an API and Chapter \@ref(evaluation) settled which numbers are
worth reporting. This chapter runs the whole thing at once.

The result is not a ranking. It is a set of curves that cross. Every method in
the grid is the best available choice somewhere on the $\theta$ axis and the
worst somewhere else, which means "method $X$ is best on crease-pattern
manifolds" has no truth value until a fold angle is attached to it. That is the
chapter's main finding, and it is a finding about benchmarking practice rather
than about any particular algorithm.

## The grid {-}

The design is a full factorial crossing of five factors, stated before any
result so that nothing below can be read as a post-hoc slice.

```{r results-design, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
design <- data.frame(
  Factor = c("Pattern", "Fold angle $\\theta$", "Noise", "Method", "Seed",
             "Metric", "Sample size", "Ambient dim.", "Target dim."),
  Levels = c(
    "`miura_ori(6, 6)`, `yoshimura(6, 6)`, `waterbomb(6, 6)`",
    "$0.0, 0.1, \\ldots, 1.4$ rad (bounded above by $\\pi/2$)",
    "none; ambient Gaussian `sd = 0.02`; outlier `sd = 0.05`",
    "`prcomp`, `cmdscale`, `vegan::isomap`, `Rtsne`, `umap`",
    "`BENCH_SEEDS` (1001–1020)",
    "`reconstruction_error`, `trustworthiness`, `continuity`, `knn_preservation`",
    "$n = 800$", "$D = 3$", "$d = 2$"
  ),
  n = c(3L, 15L, 3L, 5L, 20L, 4L, 1L, 1L, 1L)
)
knitr::kable(
  design, col.names = c("Factor", "Levels", "Count"),
  caption = "Design of the benchmark grid. The first five factors are crossed
    fully; all four metrics are computed from every fit."
)
```

Three patterns, fifteen fold angles, three noise settings, five methods and
twenty seeds give $3 \times 15 \times 3 \times 5 \times 20 = 13{,}500$ fits, each
scored on four metrics, so the committed file holds 54,000 numbers.

Two things are absent from that table and need saying rather than burying. The
`torch` autoencoder of Chapter \@ref(autoencoders) is not in the grid: it is the
only method here whose result depends on a training run rather than a
closed-form or fixed-iteration procedure, and the render workflow excludes
`torch` from the restored library to stay inside its time budget. Its numbers
come from a recorded run reported in that chapter and are not comparable to the
rest of this one. And the noise levels are what `sample_manifold()` actually
does: `sd = 0.02` ambient means isotropic Gaussian noise in $\mathbb{R}^3$,
while `sd = 0.05` outlier means two per cent of points — `round(0.02 * n)`, so
16 of the 800 — displaced by Gaussian noise of scale $0.5$, because the sampler
multiplies the supplied `sd` by ten for the points it hits. It is a small-count,
large-displacement contamination, not a five per cent perturbation.

## What the grid actually varies {-}

The pattern factor is nearly inert, and a results chapter that did not say so
would be misreporting its own design.

`miura_ori()`, `yoshimura()` and `waterbomb()` build genuinely different flat
patterns: different vertex shears, different mountain/valley assignments,
different crease topologies, all of which `plot_crease()` will draw. But
`sample_manifold()` reads only two things from the object it is handed — the
bounding box of `$vertices`, and `params$b` — and then folds an accordion along
$y$ with band width $b$. It never touches `$creases`, `$family` or `alpha`. For
the three $6 \times 6$ patterns used here, $b = 1$ in all three cases, and the
flat bounding boxes are $6.577 \times 6$, $6.5 \times 6$ and $6.5 \times 6$. The
last two are identical, so at a given seed `yoshimura(6, 6)` and
`waterbomb(6, 6)` return bit-identical `X` and `truth`; the Miura level differs
from them by a $1.2\%$ wider sampling rectangle and nothing else.

The consequence is concrete. The pattern factor contributes almost no geometric
variation, and its three levels should be read as near-replicates rather than as
a family effect. Any difference between the panels of the figures below is seed
noise plus a $1.2\%$ change in aspect ratio. Nothing in this chapter licenses a
claim that Miura-ori stresses a method differently from a waterbomb, because the
shipped sampler does not fold them differently.

What the grid does vary, and vary hard, is fold angle, noise type, method and
seed. The argument below is built on those four.

The ground-truth claim survives this intact, which is the point worth keeping.
The accordion map has unit speed within each band — $\mathrm{d}y =
\mathrm{d}u\cos\theta$, $\mathrm{d}z = \pm\,\mathrm{d}u\sin\theta$, and
$\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ — leaves $x$ untouched, and is continuous
across band boundaries. It is a genuine isometry, so `dist(m$truth)` is the
exact geodesic distance matrix of the folded surface and
`reconstruction_error()` really is measured against truth. The benchmark is
sound; it is narrower than its factor names suggest.

## Provenance {-}

`scripts/run-benchmark-grid.R` produced `data/processed/benchmark-grid.rds` and
is committed as the record of how. It is not run at render time — the full grid
takes hours, and re-running it on every build would make the figures depend on
whichever machine last touched them. It takes `--quick` for a two-seed,
two-angle smoke test, which is what continuous integration runs.

Stripped of its bookkeeping, the script is an `expand.grid()` over the design
and a loop:

```{r results-provenance}
library(foldbenchR)

PATTERNS <- list(miura     = miura_ori(6, 6),
                 yoshimura = yoshimura(6, 6),
                 waterbomb = waterbomb(6, 6))
NOISE    <- list(none    = list(type = "none",    sd = 0),
                 ambient = list(type = "ambient", sd = 0.02),
                 outlier = list(type = "outlier", sd = 0.05))
METHODS  <- list(
  pca    = function(X, d = 2) stats::prcomp(X, rank. = d)$x[, seq_len(d), drop = FALSE],
  mds    = function(X, d = 2) stats::cmdscale(stats::dist(X), k = d),
  isomap = function(X, d = 2, k = 10) tryCatch(
    vegan::isomap(stats::dist(X), ndim = d, k = k)$points[, seq_len(d), drop = FALSE],
    error = function(e) matrix(NA_real_, nrow = nrow(X), ncol = d)),
  tsne   = function(X, d = 2) Rtsne::Rtsne(X, dims = d, perplexity = 30,
                                           check_duplicates = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)$Y,
  umap   = function(X, d = 2) umap::umap(X, n_components = d)$layout
)

cells <- expand.grid(
  pattern = names(PATTERNS), theta = seq(0, 1.4, by = 0.1),
  noise = names(NOISE), seed = BENCH_SEEDS, method = names(METHODS),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)), function(i) {
  cell <- cells[i, ]
  m <- sample_manifold(PATTERNS[[cell$pattern]], theta = cell$theta, n = 800L,
                       noise = NOISE[[cell$noise]], seed = cell$seed)
  emb <- METHODS[[cell$method]](m$X)
  ok  <- is.matrix(emb) && !anyNA(emb) && nrow(emb) == nrow(m$truth)
  data.frame(
    cell,
    rmse  = if (ok) reconstruction_error(emb, m$truth) else NA_real_,
    trust = if (ok) trustworthiness(m$X, emb, k = 10)  else NA_real_,
    cont  = if (ok) continuity(m$X, emb, k = 10)       else NA_real_,
    knn   = if (ok) knn_preservation(m$X, emb, k = 10) else NA_real_
  )
}))
```

The `ok` guard is the part that matters. Isomap on a $k$-nearest-neighbour graph
can fail outright at large $\theta$, and `vegan::isomap()` can also return an
embedding of *fewer* rows than it was given when the graph splits and it keeps
the largest fragment. Either outcome records `NA` across the row rather than
aborting the loop or, worse, silently dropping the cell. Dropping failed cells
would bias every curve upward by deleting exactly the hard configurations the
benchmark exists to expose.

Every number below is read out of the committed file. The chunk that does it is
live, guarded on the file being present, and degrades to a placeholder if the
grid has not been generated on the machine doing the render.

```{r results-load, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

GRID_PATH <- "data/processed/benchmark-grid.rds"
HAVE_GRID <- file.exists(GRID_PATH)

FAMILY_LEVELS <- c("Linear", "Geodesic", "Neighbour")
FAMILY_OF <- c(pca = "Linear", mds = "Linear", isomap = "Geodesic",
               tsne = "Neighbour", umap = "Neighbour")

# An embedding carrying no information about the truth scores, after the optimal
# similarity transform, the RMS radius of the true unfolding: sqrt(2 * 6^2 / 12)
# ~ 2.4 for a 6 x 6 sheet sampled uniformly. Half of that is the convention used
# here for "broken".
BREAK_RMSE <- 1.2

read_grid <- function(path) {
  g <- readRDS(path)
  # Wide (one row per fit, one column per metric) -> long, base R only, so the
  # book does not acquire a reshaping dependency it uses nowhere else.
  id   <- intersect(c("pattern", "theta", "noise", "seed", "method"), names(g))
  mets <- setdiff(names(g), id)
  g <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mets, function(m) {
    d <- g[id]; d$metric <- m; d$value <- g[[m]]; d
  }))
  fam <- unname(FAMILY_OF[g$method])
  fam[is.na(fam)] <- "Other"
  g$family <- factor(fam, levels = c(FAMILY_LEVELS, "Other"))
  g
}

placeholder <- function(msg = "data/processed/benchmark-grid.rds not found —\nrun scripts/run-benchmark-grid.R to regenerate it") {
  ggplot() + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = msg, size = 3.4) + theme_void()
}

grid <- if (HAVE_GRID) read_grid(GRID_PATH) else NULL
```

Classical MDS is grouped with the linear family rather than with Isomap, in
spite of appearing in Chapter \@ref(geodesic). On Euclidean input
`cmdscale(dist(X))` *is* PCA up to a rotation, so its curve should coincide with
`prcomp`'s everywhere. It is carried in the grid as a control: if those two
curves ever separate, the pipeline is broken, and that is the cheapest available
check that it is not.

## The headline curve {-}

Procrustes-aligned reconstruction error is the headline metric for the reasons
given in Chapter \@ref(evaluation): of the four it is the only one measured
against truth rather than against a neighbourhood proxy in the input, and the
only one that can be zero. Figure \@ref(fig:results-rmse-curve) is the whole
benchmark — median over seeds, ribbon spanning the 10th to 90th percentile of
the seed distribution, one panel per pattern so that the near-replication of the
pattern factor is visible rather than asserted.

```{r results-rmse-curve, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Reconstruction error against fold angle theta, one panel per crease pattern, one line per method family, with ribbons for the 10th to 90th percentile across seeds. The linear family rises from zero at theta = 0 and climbs steadily. The geodesic family stays near zero until roughly theta = 1.1 and then rises steeply. The neighbour family starts near 0.3 and is almost flat across the range. The three panels are nearly identical. Families are distinguished by line type and point shape as well as colour."}
if (!HAVE_GRID) placeholder() else {
  curve <- grid |>
    filter(metric == "rmse", noise == "none") |>
    group_by(pattern, family, theta, seed) |>
    summarise(value = median(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    group_by(pattern, family, theta) |>
    summarise(md = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              lo = quantile(value, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
              hi = quantile(value, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop")

  ggplot(curve, aes(theta, md, colour = family, fill = family,
                    linetype = family, shape = family)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(size = 1.7) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = BREAK_RMSE, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.3) +
    facet_wrap(~ pattern) +
    scale_color_book() + scale_fill_book() +
    labs(x = expression(paste("fold angle ", theta, " (rad)")),
         y = "reconstruction error (RMSE)",
         colour = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL, shape = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

At $\theta = 0$ the sheet is flat, the manifold is a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and
the linear family is exact — error at the level of floating-point noise. PCA and
classical MDS agree to numerical tolerance across the whole grid, as they must.

As $\theta$ rises the linear curve leaves zero immediately and never comes back.
This is Chapter \@ref(linear)'s curve seen from the other side: variance
explained by the first two components falls because the accordion acquires
extent in $z$, and reconstruction error rises in step. There is no break point
for the linear family because there is no regime after $\theta = 0$ in which it
was doing the right thing.

Isomap is flat and near zero over most of the range. That is the expected
result and not the interesting one — a rigid fold is exactly isometric, and a
method built to recover geodesics recovers the crease pattern. The interesting
part is the right-hand end, where the curve turns up almost vertically.

The neighbour family is the mirror image: error around $0.3$ at $\theta = 0$,
far from zero on a problem where two other methods are exact, because t-SNE and
UMAP do not preserve global scale and no similarity transform can repair a
non-uniform distortion. But that error barely depends on $\theta$. A method that
is uniformly mediocre becomes the best available choice once every other curve
has risen past it.

## Where the ordering changes {-#results-regimes}

Call a family *broken* at the first $\theta$ where its median error crosses
$1.2$ — half the score an uninformative embedding earns after optimal scaling,
drawn as the dotted line in Figure \@ref(fig:results-rmse-curve). Table
\@ref(tab:results-summary) gives the break points with the error at three
reference angles.

```{r results-summary, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
if (!HAVE_GRID) {
  knitr::kable(
    data.frame(Note = "benchmark-grid.rds not found — run scripts/run-benchmark-grid.R"),
    caption = "Per-family summary: median reconstruction error at three fold
      angles, the share of cells that failed to embed, and the smallest theta at
      which the median crosses the break threshold of 1.2."
  )
} else {
  summ <- grid |>
    filter(metric == "rmse", noise == "none") |>
    group_by(family, theta) |>
    summarise(md = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              na_frac = mean(is.na(value)), .groups = "drop")

  fams <- levels(droplevels(summ$family))
  at <- function(f, t) summ$md[match(paste(f, t), paste(summ$family, summ$theta))]
  wide <- data.frame(
    family      = fams,
    t0          = vapply(fams, at, numeric(1), t = 0.0),
    t07         = vapply(fams, at, numeric(1), t = 0.7),
    t14         = vapply(fams, at, numeric(1), t = 1.4),
    na_pct      = vapply(fams, function(f)
                    100 * mean(summ$na_frac[summ$family == f]), numeric(1)),
    theta_break = vapply(fams, function(f) {
                    b <- summ$theta[summ$family == f & summ$md > BREAK_RMSE]
                    if (length(b)) min(b) else NA_real_
                  }, numeric(1))
  )

  knitr::kable(
    wide, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("Family", "$\\theta = 0$", "$\\theta = 0.7$", "$\\theta = 1.4$",
                  "Failed (%)", "Break $\\theta$"),
    caption = "Per-family summary: median reconstruction error at three fold
      angles, the share of cells that failed to embed, and the smallest theta at
      which the median crosses the break threshold of 1.2. `NA` in the last
      column means the family never crosses it inside the grid."
  )
}
```

The linear family fails by erosion: degraded from the first step, no transition,
just a monotone climb. Isomap fails the opposite way — flat, near-perfect, then
a cliff — and the cliff has an arithmetic explanation that the grid confirms
rather than discovers.

The folded accordion places adjacent bands $b\cos\theta$ apart in $y$. Sampling
$n = 800$ points uniformly over a sheet of area $\approx 39.5$ gives density
$\lambda \approx 20.3$, so the distance to the tenth nearest neighbour is about
$\sqrt{k / \pi\lambda} \approx 0.40$. Bridging edges between adjacent bands
appear once $b\cos\theta$ falls below that radius, at $\cos\theta \approx 0.40$,
$\theta \approx 1.16$. The first grid point above that is $\theta = 1.2$, and
that is where Isomap's curve turns. One bridging edge is enough: it collapses a
geodesic estimate spanning a whole band, and the shortest-path matrix stops
being an isometry of the flat sheet.

`short_circuit_theta()` from Chapter \@ref(geodesic) answers a blunter question
and returns a later angle. Its criterion is an ambient neighbour whose *true*
separation exceeds the median pairwise true distance, roughly $3.2$ on this
sheet, which needs bridging across three bands rather than one — $3.2\cos\theta <
0.40$, so $\theta > 1.44$. The two numbers are not in conflict. Geodesic
estimates start degrading well before any single edge is long enough to trip a
median-based detector, and a benchmark that reported only the detector's angle
would place the failure too late by a quarter of a radian.

```{r results-rank-flip, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.6, fig.alt="Median rank of each method family by reconstruction error against fold angle, with rank 1 at the top. The linear family starts at rank 1 and drops to rank 2 then 3 as theta rises. The geodesic family climbs to rank 1 by theta = 0.2 and holds it until it drops sharply near theta = 1.2. The neighbour family starts at rank 3 and reaches rank 1 at the high-theta end. Lines cross twice; families are distinguished by line type and point shape as well as colour."}
if (!HAVE_GRID) placeholder() else {
  ranks <- grid |>
    filter(metric == "rmse", noise == "none") |>
    group_by(pattern, theta, family) |>
    summarise(md = median(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(md = ifelse(is.na(md), Inf, md)) |>
    group_by(pattern, theta) |>
    mutate(rank = rank(md, ties.method = "min")) |>
    group_by(theta, family) |>
    summarise(rank = median(rank), .groups = "drop")

  ggplot(ranks, aes(theta, rank, colour = family, linetype = family,
                    shape = family)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:3) +
    scale_color_book() +
    labs(x = expression(paste("fold angle ", theta, " (rad)")),
         y = "median rank (1 = best)",
         colour = NULL, linetype = NULL, shape = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

Figure \@ref(fig:results-rank-flip) drops the magnitudes and keeps the ordering,
which is the part most benchmark tables report. There are three regimes. Below
about $\theta = 0.15$ the linear family wins outright. From roughly $0.2$ to
$1.1$ Isomap wins, by a margin large enough that no amount of seed variation
touches it. Above about $1.2$ the neighbour family wins — not by improving, but
by standing still while the others collapse. Every pairwise ordering in the grid
reverses at least once across the sweep.

That is why this chapter opens by refusing to give a ranking. A benchmark
reporting one number per method has silently fixed a difficulty level, and which
method it crowns is a property of that choice. State the fold angle, or make no
claim.

## Distributions, not means {-}

Twenty seeds per cell exist so that differences can be tested rather than
eyeballed. Figure \@ref(fig:results-seed-spread) shows the seed distribution at
three fold angles instead of a summary of it.

```{r results-seed-spread, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Boxplots with overlaid points of reconstruction error across twenty seeds for each of the five methods, at fold angles 0, 0.7 and 1.4 radians. At theta = 0 the PCA and classical MDS boxes sit on zero with no visible spread while t-SNE and UMAP show wide boxes. At theta = 0.7 Isomap has the lowest median. At theta = 1.4 the Isomap box has moved above the t-SNE and UMAP boxes and is much wider."}
if (!HAVE_GRID) placeholder() else {
  slice <- grid |>
    filter(metric == "rmse", noise == "none", theta %in% c(0.0, 0.7, 1.4))

  ggplot(slice, aes(reorder(method, value, FUN = function(v) median(v, na.rm = TRUE)),
                    value, colour = family, shape = family)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.1, na.rm = TRUE) +
    facet_wrap(~ theta, labeller = label_bquote(theta == .(theta))) +
    scale_color_book() +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "reconstruction error (RMSE)",
         colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

The spreads are not decoration. A great deal of the between-method variation in
this grid falls inside within-method seed variance, and the honest way to report
that is a ratio: the gap between two methods' medians over the pooled standard
deviation of a single method's error across seeds. Table
\@ref(tab:results-resolvability) computes it for adjacent pairs in the ranking.

```{r results-resolvability, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
if (!HAVE_GRID) {
  knitr::kable(
    data.frame(Note = "benchmark-grid.rds not found — run scripts/run-benchmark-grid.R"),
    caption = "Resolvability of adjacent method pairs: median gap in
      reconstruction error over the pooled across-seed standard deviation.
      Values near or below 1 mark comparisons that twenty seeds cannot settle."
  )
} else {
  res <- grid |>
    filter(metric == "rmse", noise == "none",
           theta %in% c(0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.4)) |>
    group_by(theta, method) |>
    summarise(md = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(theta, md) |>
    group_by(theta) |>
    mutate(pair   = paste(lag(method), "vs", method),
           gap    = md - lag(md),
           pooled = sqrt((sd^2 + lag(sd)^2) / 2),
           ratio  = gap / pooled) |>
    ungroup() |>
    filter(!is.na(gap)) |>
    select(theta, pair, gap, pooled, ratio)

  knitr::kable(
    res, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("$\\theta$", "Adjacent pair", "Median gap", "Pooled SD",
                  "Gap / SD"),
    caption = "Resolvability of adjacent method pairs: median gap in
      reconstruction error over the pooled across-seed standard deviation.
      Values near or below 1 mark comparisons that twenty seeds cannot settle."
  )
}
```

Two patterns recur there. The PCA-to-MDS gap is identically zero to numerical
tolerance, which is the control firing as designed. And t-SNE and UMAP are never
separated by much more than a pooled standard deviation at any fold angle: they
differ, but not by enough for twenty seeds to say which is ahead, and a paper
reporting a winner between them from a single run is reporting a seed. The
Isomap-to-PCA gap through the middle of the range, by contrast, is several times
the pooled spread and needs no hedging.

A benchmark that resolves large differences and admits it cannot resolve small
ones is behaving correctly. The failure mode to avoid is one that reports a
crisp ranking of everything.

Failures are part of the distribution too. Cells where Isomap could not embed
carry `NA` rather than a value, and the failure share in Table
\@ref(tab:results-summary) is itself a result: at low $\theta$ it is zero, and it
rises with the same geometry that drives the break. Treating those cells as
missing at random — dropping them and taking the median of what is left — would
report Isomap as accurate precisely where it has stopped working.

## Noise {-}

Noise moves the levels without changing that structure. Ambient Gaussian noise
at $\sigma = 0.02$ lifts every curve by roughly a constant and pulls Isomap's
break in by about a grid step, because displacement perpendicular to the surface
brings bands into each other's neighbourhoods sooner. The outlier setting is the
one that separates the families: sixteen points thrown out by a displacement of
scale $0.5$ barely touch PCA, are absorbed by t-SNE and UMAP, and cost Isomap
disproportionately, because an outlier parked between two bands is exactly the
short-circuit edge the method cannot tolerate. Robustness to outliers and
sensitivity to fold angle are different axes, and a method can be good on one
and bad on the other.

## Per family {-}

**Linear (Chapter \@ref(linear)).** Exact at $\theta = 0$, monotonically worse
after, no tuning, no seed dependence, and cheaper than everything else by three
orders of magnitude. It fails in a way that is completely predictable from the
geometry, which is more than can be said for the rest. Classical MDS reproduces
it exactly, as the theory says it must.

**Geodesic (Chapter \@ref(geodesic)).** The strongest result and the sharpest
failure. Isomap recovers the fold to near machine precision over most of the
range and then falls off a cliff at the fold angle where the neighbourhood
radius overtakes the band spacing — an angle predictable in advance from $n$,
$k$ and $b$, which is the closest thing this book has to a validated model of a
method's failure. Locally linear embedding, which Chapter \@ref(geodesic) also
covers, is not in this grid.

**Neighbour (Chapter \@ref(neighbor)).** Never good, never catastrophic. Both
t-SNE and UMAP produce embeddings that look like a folded sheet and score badly
against it, which is the most useful thing this benchmark has to say about them:
here, visual plausibility and reconstruction error are close to uncorrelated.
They are also not separable from each other at twenty seeds at any fold angle,
so the perennial t-SNE-versus-UMAP question is, on this benchmark, not a
question.

**Learned (Chapter \@ref(autoencoders)).** Absent from the grid, for the reason
given above. The autoencoder is also the only method with an explicit inverse,
and the grid scores encoder output only — so even when its numbers are folded
in, they will not test the fold-and-unfold claim that chapter is actually about.
Nothing here should be read as evidence for or against it.

## What it costs {-}

Wall-clock decides what anyone actually runs, so it is reported, with the
caveats that timings always need. The grid file does not carry a timing column;
the numbers below come from a separate instrumented sweep over the same
configurations, measured as

```{r results-timing-code}
timed <- function(f, X) {
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  f(X)
  proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
}
```

```{r results-cost, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.2, fig.alt="Median wall-clock seconds per fit for each method at n = 800, on a logarithmic scale. PCA is fastest at a few milliseconds, classical MDS takes about a third of a second, t-SNE and Isomap take a few seconds, and UMAP is slowest at around five seconds. Methods are ordered by cost and marked by family with distinct point shapes."}
cost <- data.frame(
  method = c("pca", "mds", "tsne", "isomap", "umap"),
  family = factor(c("Linear", "Linear", "Neighbour", "Geodesic", "Neighbour"),
                  levels = c("Linear", "Geodesic", "Neighbour")),
  secs   = c(0.004, 0.34, 2.0, 2.6, 5.2)
)

ggplot(cost, aes(reorder(method, secs), secs, colour = family, shape = family)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = reorder(method, secs), y = 0.002, yend = secs),
               linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_book() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "median seconds per fit (n = 800, log scale)",
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The spread is roughly three orders of magnitude, from milliseconds for `prcomp`
to several seconds for `umap`. Summed over 13,500 fits the grid is most of a day
on one core, which is why it is precomputed and committed rather than rendered.

Scaling with $n$ was measured over $n \in \{200, 400, 800, 1600\}$ at fixed
$\theta$, as the slope of $\log(\text{seconds})$ on $\log n$. The dense steps —
the $n \times n$ distance matrix that both `cmdscale` and `isomap` require, and
the eigendecomposition after it — come out between $2.2$ and $2.6$. The
neighbour methods sit near $1.2$, consistent with the Barnes–Hut and approximate
nearest-neighbour implementations doing what they advertise. `prcomp` is linear.

Four caveats, since timings invite over-reading. They are wall-clock on one
machine, single-threaded except where the BLAS decided otherwise, and include R
call overhead, which dominates at the `prcomp` end where the measurement is
smaller than the noise. They cover the fit only, not sampling or scoring. They
are default settings — `umap`'s cost in particular is a function of
`n_neighbors` and epoch count, neither of which was tuned. And four points is
enough to distinguish $O(n)$ from $O(n^{2.5})$ and nowhere near enough to
distinguish $O(n^2)$ from $O(n^2\log n)$.

## What the grid does not cover {-#results-limits}

The honest reading of any benchmark is bounded by its design, so the boundaries
are listed rather than left implied.

The fold is an accordion. Every pattern level is folded by the same one-degree-
of-freedom zig-zag along $y$, so the grid tests one folded geometry at fifteen
fold angles, not three geometries. A genuine Miura-ori zig-zags in $x$ as well
and has two crease families; nothing here measures what that does to a method.
Extending `sample_manifold()` to fold from `$creases` rather than from the row
index is the single change that would most improve this benchmark.

Intrinsic dimension is $2$ and ambient dimension is $3$ throughout. The
`fold_product()` and `lift()` constructions of Chapter \@ref(benchmarks) —
intrinsic $2k$ in ambient $3k$, and orthonormal lifts to arbitrary $D$ — are not
in this grid, which is the largest gap after the accordion. Several of these
methods behave differently once the ambient dimension is high enough for
distance concentration to matter, and none of that is tested here.

Sample size is fixed at $n = 800$, and Isomap's break angle is a function of it:
denser sampling shrinks the neighbourhood radius and pushes the cliff to larger
$\theta$; sparser sampling pulls it in. The break angles reported above are
properties of this grid, not of Isomap.

Each method appears at one hyperparameter setting — $k = 10$ for Isomap and for
the metrics, perplexity $30$ for t-SNE, package defaults for `umap`. These are
defaults, not optima, and a per-cell tuned version of any method would sit above
its curve here. Chapter \@ref(neighbor) sweeps perplexity and `n_neighbors`
separately; those sweeps are not folded into this grid. Target dimension is
fixed at $2$, which is the case the book is about and not the case anyone should
always be in.

Noise is three settings, one of them none, with no on-manifold noise — the
sampler supports `type = "manifold"` and the grid does not use it — and no
non-uniform sampling density. Folding is rigid, so paper stretch, facet bending
and self-intersection are outside the model entirely. And the input metric is
Euclidean throughout, with no test of what happens when the metric itself is
wrong, which on real data it usually is.

Chapter \@ref(comparison) asks whether any of this could have been learned from
a Swiss roll. Chapter \@ref(application) takes the crossover structure found
here and tries to turn it into a method choice for a dataset with no answer key.
